$comment: Projection vectors: an expose schema plus one row, and the exact canonical NDJSON line KERNEL-SPEC §8's line(row) must produce for it. Every `line` here is written by hand from §8 and §9, not captured from the implementation, so a transcription error in either side is a failure. Values are encoded with single-key `$`-tagged objects so a JSON file can carry the Python value classes §9 renders from: $decimal (an exact decimal string), $date (YYYY-MM-DD), $datetime (an RFC 3339 string handed to the renderer as a datetime), $bytes (base64 of the raw bytes), $ms (integer milliseconds since the epoch), $tuple (a sequence). Anything else is the JSON value itself. Driven by tests/seam/test_vectors.py.

encoding.$ms: int(<integer>) -- milliseconds since the Unix epoch

vectors.name: telco payment_recovery_moment, the shipped schema
telco schema, an absent optional column renders as JSON null
the row is an array in declared order, not an object
vectors.why: JCS sorts object keys, so an object would have emitted alpha first. §8 uses arrays for exactly this reason.

vectors.name: the same two columns declared the other way round
STRING renders NFC, and the decomposed spelling becomes the composed one
JCS emits raw UTF-8, not backslash escapes
a control character in a STRING is escaped by JCS
vectors.why: The newline inside the value is escaped, so exactly one raw newline terminates the line -- which is what makes the NDJSON framing unambiguous.

vectors.name: an astral-plane character survives as raw UTF-8
INT renders as a JSON integer, never as a string
DECIMAL renders as a string at the declared scale
vectors.why: A DECIMAL is a string, so JCS never puts it through the IEEE 754 double domain.

vectors.name: a decimal at the declared scale keeps its trailing zeros
negative zero folds onto the positive spelling
vectors.why: -0.00 and 0.00 are one number; two spellings would be two digests.

vectors.name: rounding is half-to-even, the rounding a SQL cast applies
BOOL renders as a JSON bool
DATE renders YYYY-MM-DD, from a date or from a string
TIMESTAMP renders RFC 3339 UTC with milliseconds and Z
vectors.why: An offset is normalised to UTC, so two spellings of one instant are one value.

vectors.name: JSON renders as the canonical JSON string of its value
vectors.why: The nested document is canonicalised (keys sorted by JCS) and the result is carried as a string, so the outer array's own canonicalisation cannot re-sort it.

vectors.name: a decimal inside a JSON column stays an exact string
BYTES renders as base64
every logical type in one row
a row of nothing but nulls in optional columns
an explicit null in an optional column
a single-column expose
a positional row is taken in declared order
an integer at the top of the JCS safe domain
vectors.why: 2^53 - 1: the largest integer with a canonical JCS spelling.

vectors.name: a decimal far outside the double domain stays exact
vectors.why: A decimal is a string, so no rounding to a double can happen to it.

vectors.name: the earliest and latest timestamps the clock renders in four digits

rejections.name: a float value
rejections.why: KERNEL-SPEC §9: float -> FLX-3002. A binary float has no reproducible spelling.

rejections.name: a float in a column whose type is not numeric at all
rejections.why: The float check runs before type dispatch, so a float is a float everywhere.

rejections.name: a float nested inside a JSON column
rejections.why: The check is recursive: a JSON column is not a place a float can hide.

rejections.name: an undeclared column
rejections.why: The seam is closed-world; the emitted array is positional and an undeclared value has no position.

rejections.name: a required column that is absent
rejections.why: KERNEL-SPEC §9: a row missing a required column -> FLX-3202.

rejections.name: a required column that is present as null
rejections.why: A required column whose value is null carries no value.

rejections.name: a positional row shorter than the declared column set
rejections.why: Rows are aligned to the header; a row of another length has no alignment.

rejections.name: a positional row longer than the declared column set
rejections.why: The same rule in the other direction.

rejections.name: a string where an INT is declared
rejections.why: The seam renders from a closed set of value classes so the spelling is a function of the declaration alone.

rejections.name: a bool where an INT is declared
rejections.why: bool is a subclass of int in Python and a different type in JSON; the seam follows JSON.

rejections.name: a decimal too large for its declared precision
rejections.why: DECIMAL(4,2) admits two integer digits; rounding cannot make three fit.

rejections.name: a date spelled some other ISO 8601 way
rejections.why: §9's rendering is YYYY-MM-DD, so a string input is required to already be spelled that way.

rejections.name: a timestamp with no offset
rejections.why: A timestamp with no offset names no instant.

rejections.name: an already-base64 string where BYTES is declared
rejections.why: The seam does the base64, so a caller passing base64 would produce a doubly-encoded value.

schemaRejections.name: a float column type
schemaRejections.why: Refused at the declaration, not at every row: a float column has no §9 rendering.

schemaRejections.name: an unparameterised decimal
schemaRejections.why: §9's set member is DECIMAL(p,s); a default scale here would silently decide how every number in the stream is spelled.

schemaRejections.name: a type outside FLUID's own vocabulary
schemaRejections.why: The closed set has no member for it.

schemaRejections.name: two columns whose names normalise together
schemaRejections.why: NFC makes them one name, and one name cannot have two positions.

schemaRejections.name: an empty schema
schemaRejections.why: There is no ordered column set to align rows to.
